classification.difficultyReason: Apply repeated halving to a quantity over five nights and explain why a positive remainder persists.

inlines.text: Johan found a 4-litre tub of ice cream. He stopped when he had eaten half of it.
The next night he again stopped when he had eaten half of what was there.
This went on for five nights in a row.
How much ice cream was left at the end of each of the five nights?
Would he ever have finished all the ice cream?

answer.short: Nights 1–5: $2\text{ L}$, $1\text{ L}$, $\frac12\text{ L}$, $\frac14\text{ L}$, $\frac18\text{ L}$. No; each night leaves half of the positive amount remaining.
answer.worked:
Half of the remaining ice cream is left each night.
$$\begin{align*}
\text{Night 1}&: 4\times\frac12=2\text{ L}\\
\text{Night 2}&: 2\times\frac12=1\text{ L}\\
\text{Night 3}&: 1\times\frac12=\frac12\text{ L}\\
\text{Night 4}&: \frac12\times\frac12=\frac14\text{ L}\\
\text{Night 5}&: \frac14\times\frac12=\frac18\text{ L}
\end{align*}$$
After night $n$, the amount left is $4\times\left(\frac12\right)^n\text{ L}$. No; repeated halving always leaves a positive amount, so the ice cream never runs out under this process.
